source.title: Scaling Laws for Generative Reward Models
source.authors: Angel Raychev; Nathan Lile; Rafael Rafailov

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no truncation or garbling apparent.
record.tranche_reason: Extends scale-related evaluation to generative reward models used for online DPO policy optimization, rather than testing held-out pretraining cross-entropy laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports rewarder- and policy-size sweeps and post-hoc fits of Gold Elo. These measure downstream outcomes in a different training regime; they do not measure held-out pretraining loss, training tokens, compute-optimal allocation, or architecture shape. The text also reports static GenRM accuracy, but that is not a direct test of pretraining-loss scaling. Its cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Only the policy-size sweep bears on V6. It trains Qwen3 policies of 0.6B–8B with online DPO under a fixed 4B rewarder and reports how quality under a learned 32B Gold evaluator changes with policy size. This is a post-training creative-writing outcome, not pretraining loss. The rewarder-size sweeps scale a different model (the judge), not the evaluated system, so they fit no version. The paper's log-size fits are in-sample summaries that the authors say are not predictive laws.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The central finding is an evaluator–rewarder gap. Thinking GRPO judges have higher static Gold-label accuracy, yet Answer-Only SFT judges train better policies in 7 of 8 matched settings. Intermediate judge checkpoints can beat later, more accurate ones as rewarders. Rewarder scale is a major driver of Gold-rated outcomes, even above policy size. All results are conditional on a learned Gold reference, and the size fits are descriptive, not scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales Qwen3 generative rewarders and policies in online DPO and measures Gold Elo, rather than measuring held-out pretraining cross-entropy, token count, or training compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes depend on rewarder mode/training recipe (Answer-Only SFT versus Thinking GRPO), rewarder size, policy size, training duration, and the learned Gold evaluator. Thinking trajectories and size effects are less monotonic; evaluator-specific ratings are separate fits.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing rewarder (GenRM) size raises the Gold Elo of a fixed 4B policy. Answer-Only gains are monotone (14B: 1630); Thinking gains are non-monotone (8B 1488 > 14B 1437). Fitted at about 136 and 116 Elo per judge doubling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reward-model scale improves downstream policy quality in online preference optimization, including judges larger than the policy.

fits_no_version.finding: At a matched 12B parameter sum, Answer-Only favors the 8B-policy/4B-judge split (1645.0 vs 1513.1), while Thinking favors the 4B-policy/8B-judge split (1488.1 vs 1402.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The best policy/rewarder parameter split depends on the rewarder's training pipeline.

fits_no_version.finding: Static GenRM accuracy on Gold labels rises with judge size, but static accuracy does not predict rewarder quality: the 250-step judge (79.2%) beats the 300-step judge (82.3%) as a rewarder.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Static evaluator accuracy does not determine online rewarder quality.

record.code_released: not stated (the text says the public research repository contains the code and analysis, but gives no URL)
record.problems: The work uses one model family (Qwen3), one principal creative-writing setting, and a learned Gold reference rather than direct human evaluation. The scale grid is sparse and not averaged across independent seeds; the post-hoc fits are in-sample, and the authors state they are not predictive scaling laws. Bootstrap intervals cover stored comparison rows only, not prompt clusters, fresh generations, retraining, or evaluator changes. Some plotted trajectory values are not available as exact numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted within the recorded scale outcomes. The separately reported peak-Elo summaries in Table 4 were not given separate rows because the extracted per-configuration rows use the top-five-average Gold Elo metric; Table 4 reports both metrics for its listed configurations.

untested.parts: No extrapolation from small to large runs; the fits are in-sample only.
No compute-optimal allocation. The 12B parameter-sum swap is not a compute budget.
No power-law loss fit in another modality or regime. Online DPO outcomes are Elo, not loss.
Out-of-sample prediction, pretraining loss as a predictor, standard benchmark suites, other model families.
No comparison of fitting choices or of published exponents.

missing.what: Top-five Gold Elo for the 8B policy with the 4B Thinking rewarder (1402.2)
Peak-Elo fit coefficients: Answer-Only policy 186.0 per doubling, Thinking policy 113.3 per doubling, R2 0.954
Per-configuration peak Gold Elo values (e.g. 8B Answer-Only policy 1736)

record.verdict_notes: The paper's title invokes scaling laws, but it does not test pretraining-loss scaling. Linking V6 rests only on the policy-size sweep, where the measured quantity is creative-writing quality under a learned judge after online DPO, with one run per cell and no seeds. A stricter reading would treat the whole study as fitting no version. R3 and R11 are the same run.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power laws across modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.

The study measures Gold-evaluated online policy outcomes against rewarder and policy size, but does not test pretraining loss as a predictor, broad downstream task suites, or out-of-sample prediction.
It gives caveats about its sparse post-hoc fit, but does not test disagreement among published pretraining exponents, parameter-counting choices, or bending of pretraining loss curves.

relationships.condition: Policy-size sweep with a fixed 4B Thinking rewarder
relationships.reason: Gains are weaker (119 Elo per doubling). Larger policies peak earlier and decline, so the size benefit depends on training duration and checkpoint choice (R5–R8, R20).
relationships.display_finding: Performance improved by 119 Elo per policy-size doubling, but larger policies peaked earlier and then declined, making gains depend on training duration and checkpoint selection.

relation.reason: The study directly varies policy size and measures downstream Gold Elo, bearing on V6.

tranche.reason: The policy-size sweep tests downstream scaling in a new setting: creative-writing online DPO evaluated by a learned Gold reference.

source_check.notes: Figures 6 and 14 use different arena arrangements; their ratings are not interchangeable. Fits are descriptive, checkpoint-selected and conditional on a learned Gold evaluator, without independent-seed or out-of-sample validation.

statements.correction: Fixed 4B Thinking rewarder; Qwen3 policies 0.6B–8B; 0.6B and 1.7B peak near the recorded window's end; 4B peaks around step 320; 8B peaks around step 130 and subsequently declines; largest policy has highest peak; V6 limits_scope for dependence on duration and checkpoint selection.
statements.problem: The study-specific trajectory description is correct, but its challenges classification overstates the evidence. Earlier decline with training does not establish absent or reversed policy-size benefits; the largest Thinking-supervised policy achieves the highest peak in its policy-size arena.
